en: The Sūtra on the Ritual for the Accomplishment of Visualization of the Vajrapāṇi-cakra from the Great Teaching of the Yoga of Mañjuśrī,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
Translated by the Imperial Subject Dharma-bhadra, the Great Master Mingjiao, by Imperial Decree. Part One: The Maṇḍala Section. At that time, Vajrapāṇi...
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings,
I shall now expound the methods for accomplishing all [attainments]."
"May the Buddha, out of great compassion, grant me fearlessness.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, Peḷava!
For the sake of benefiting others, speak as you wish."
Then, having received the Buddha’s command,
Pīlava immediately manifested a great and terrifying form within the assembly of all devas and humans,
and expounded the methods for accomplishing all siddhis.
If there is a vidyādhara who wishes to practice this dharma of mine,
they should first [direct their intention] toward all sentient beings.
Having generated a mind of vast benefit,
one should seek and receive initiation from a Vajrācārya; once initiation has been obtained,
one must then accomplish various rites according to the ritual manual with certainty.
Furthermore, when a vidyādhara sees sentient beings of evil karma who defy royal decrees,
willfully cause chaos and disorder, and are unfilial toward their parents;
They harbor malice toward their ācāryas and elders;
they destroy the Three Jewels and slander the Mahāyāna and secret teachings;
and with a disrespectful mind, they transgress samādhi.
If there are sentient beings who suddenly give rise to harmful intent toward others,
such persons should be subdued by means of this method. Alternatively,
if they attain a mind of repentance, one should provide them with an explanation.
Furthermore, the vidyādhara must not harbor ignorance, malice, or envy within his own mind;
he should be one who possesses manifold virtues toward all sentient beings.
Whoever repeatedly performs such acts as these to cause affliction and harm will,
in the future, experience their karmic fruit by entering the Great Hell of Screaming,
where they shall undergo manifold sufferings for immeasurable eons.
A vidyādhara must distance himself from such faults and evils before he may practice the construction of a maṇḍala and seek various accomplishments.
One who wishes to construct a maṇḍala...
First, one must select an excellent site.
An excellent site refers to before an image of Maheśvara,
or on a mountain peak, or in an empty house.
Whether at a shrine to the devas, or a temple to the mātṛs,
or a śītavana cemetery, or on a riverbank,
or beneath a great tree, or at a site of a great battle.
Whether at a crossroads or within a village,
having selected such excellent locations,
one then constructs a maṇḍala upon that ground to seek various accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The Dharma refers to the rites for pacifying calamities (*śāntika*), increasing prosperity (*pauṣṭika*), magnetizing (*vaśīkaraṇa*), and subjugating (*abhicāruka*),
as well as the rites for dispatching [spirits] and binding [them],
and furthermore, the pursuit of sacred medicines, sacred swords, and eye-salves.
He enters the dragon palaces for sacred medicines and extracts hidden treasures;
furthermore, he subdues vetālas, piśācas, yakṣas, and yakṣiṇīs.
Even down to such rites as the subduing of dragons,
if a vidyādhara applies himself single-mindedly to these various dharmas according to the ritual procedures, he will certainly attain accomplishment.
Furthermore, when a vidyādhara constructs a maṇḍala, he should,
upon the previously obtained superior site,
proceed according to the method of the mahiṣamukha [rite].
At night, in a śītavana cemetery,
one should go naked with disheveled hair and construct a square maṇḍala using funeral ashes, making four gates and a multi-storied pavilion above them.
Adorned with various ornaments such as vajra-jewels,
crescent moons, and even bells, banners, streamers, and flower garlands,
one should draw an eight-spoked wheel at the center of the maṇḍala.
Divide the center of the wheel into nine positions, forming the shape of a full moon;
leave only one gate open while the remaining gates are depicted as closed.
In the center of the wheel, place a śava.
In the eastern position, place Śmaśāna; in the southern position, place Hāstaka;
in the western position, place Aṭavī;
and in the northern position, place Parnaśavarī.
In the northeast corner, place Karpūra;
in the southeast corner, place Caṣaka;
and in the southwest corner, place Somaśanakalpaṭa.
In the northwest corner, one should place Śūlapāṇi;
with such a symbol, he is placed within the wheel.
Next, outside the wheel, in the eastern direction...
In the east, one should place Aṅkatarpiṇī, Parāvasarocakagaṇayaṃkuśa, and so forth;
in the south, Aṅkuśarāśraghanakṣuṇṇagajagrāsa, and so forth.
In the west, one should place Vajranarmaruca-kṣataka-danu-khaṇḍa-marda-karbaṭa;
in the north, one should place Tāri-jñānadevi-pātaka-gaja-cari-vajra-mudgara-kunta-agni-kunta, and so forth.
At the four gates and the four corners,
one should install Mahāvetālas; for this,
one should use mahāśveta oil to light lamps.
They feed upon *nara*, *khara*, *uṣṭra*, *śṛgāla*, *mahiṣa*, *gaja*, *aśva*, *miṣa*, *mṛga*, *sūkara*, and so forth, as well as various kinds of corpses.
Offer the maṇḍala.
Furthermore, use *kṛtāruka-karkaśa-nāga-sthitāsara-samayara-mahendra-mahāśakuna*, etc., along with *piśita* (flesh), as food.
Furthermore, one should offer the maṇḍala.
Thus, when making the food offering, the vidyādhara should apply himself with a devout and single-minded mind.
Even when performing the homa, all that arises is likewise so.
Furthermore, outside the maṇḍala,
one should everywhere perform the purification with rudrākṣa.
The Vidyādhara, having thus received the upavāsa vows according to the Mahiṣamukha rite,
must together with his companions— making four in all—
remain constantly focused and never indolent.
Only the Vidyādhara alone shall smear his body with vairocana,
remain naked with disheveled hair,
and at midnight hold a nāmaruka in his hand.
Striking out a loud sound,
the vidyādhara utters "He-he" and enters the maṇḍala with fierce concentration.
In order to achieve accomplishment,
the vidyādhara, having established the human maṇḍala according to the ritual,
then uses the food previously prepared.
One should offer to the tutelary deity Mahāvajrapāla.
That vidyādhara then visualizes Vajrapāla within the maṇḍala.
Having received the offerings of food and drink presented by them,
and having thus visualized the attainment [of the deity] as being present before him, the vidyādhara stands before the maṇḍala.
With the body assuming the posture of a leftward dance and displaying the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*),
recite the ten-syllable Great Mantra with single-minded concentration without interruption,
until Peḷava appears in his own form.
If, during this interval, various demonic manifestations appear—
frightening signs intended to create obstacles—
the vidyādhara must not feel fear.
If one has a fearful mind, Māra will immediately find an opportunity and cause the sought-after dharma to fail to be accomplished; however,
when there is no fear, [Māra finds no such opportunity].
The Vajrapāla appeared with joy and addressed the vidyādhara, saying:
"What boon do you seek? I shall grant it to you now."
The Vidyādhara said:
"I seek the noble sword and entry into the nāga palace;
I pray that you grant me various sacred medicines and other such things."
Then Peḷava said to the vidyādhara,
"I shall grant you everything that you seek.
At that time, the vidyādhara may have lacked merit.
For one who does not attain accomplishment in such superior dharmas, accomplishment will still be attained in those of middling and inferior degree. 2.
Regarding the section on all methods of accomplishment, the second part: when a vidyādhara wishes to perform the rite of subjugation (*tāḍana*) or *śatru* (enmity), [he should proceed as follows].
First, visualize oneself as the Great Wrathful Vajrapāṇi,
or as Śumbha, according to the Mahiṣamukha ritual method.
Take a shroud from a corpse and mix it with poisonous drugs, blood, salt, mustard seeds,
the juice of *kirimāla* wood, and the juice of *mandārava* flowers to create the pigments.
Use a crow’s wing as a brush.
Upon the shroud over the aforementioned corpse, draw the Vajraprāvaraṇa maṇḍala.
Within it, divide the space into sixteen positions,
with the central position occupied by an image of Prāvaraṇa.
Facing south, naked and with hair loose,
one should draw two fire pits before this image;
between the two pits, one should write the name of Śatru.
Furthermore, write the ten-syllable Great Illumination mantra as a boundary,
with the name in the center.
Again, write eight *hūṃ* syllables surrounding that name.
Furthermore, write the syllable *phaṭ* in the four corners.
Having written them thus, place them inside the skull and cover it with another skull.
Afterwards, construct a triangular furnace.
Place skulls at the top and bottom,
and use firewood from cremated corpses to kindle the flames and burn them.
The Vidyādhara assumes the aforementioned form of the Great Wrathful One,
treads upon a skull with his left foot,
and recites the ten-syllable Great Mantra.
That *setuḍa* will be swiftly and suddenly extinguished.
Furthermore, as before, one should compound various medicinal substances and write the name of the *setuḍa* upon a shroud from a corpse.
Furthermore, add the Great Illumination Mantra of thirty-two syllables and write it encircling the name.
Also, use the remains of *kāka-carcā* (crow-food) and *vairūḍhaka*.
Smear it upon one's clothing and later bury it in a śītavana (charnel ground); thus,
the śatru (enemy) shall also be swiftly eliminated.
If buried beneath a large tree, it will immediately be dispatched.
If placed before an image of Maheśvara, one will quickly suffer the pain of separation from loved ones.
If submerged at the bottom of water, it will immediately be suppressed.
If one performs the rite for pacifying calamities within the house,
one should take that garment, wash it thoroughly, and treat it in all respects as usual.
Furthermore, the vidyādhara takes the shroud from the corpse.
Having written the mantra of Yama,
[one should place it] in a śītavana cemetery, at a crossroads,
beneath a great tree, or between two mounds of white ant earth.
One should take earth from such places as before an image of Maheśvara or before the gate of a royal palace;
furthermore, one uses *vairūḍhaka* (*vajranāga*) and charcoal from a cremation ground.
Together with the assistant, fashion a form of Dhṛtarāṣṭra eight finger-widths in length.
Place the aforementioned Great Mantra within its heart.
Furthermore, at five locations on the body,
he drives in stakes made of human bone;
he also uses thorns to pierce the various parts and joints of the body.
Having pierced it all over, place it inside a skull and cover it with another skull.
Then, at either midday or midnight, take [the substance].
At seven locations, take earth from an anthill and fashion a figure of Yama one cubit in height with a most terrifying countenance;
it has two arms, the right hand holding a sword, and its hair is disheveled.
Within this heart of Yama, one should install the form of Cakrin; then,
at either midnight or midday, [one should proceed].
In the pit where the corpse was cremated,
he should bury it deeply with the head facing south and the face turned downward;
then the vidyādhara shall return to his own abode.
Recite the ten-syllable vidyā-mantra according to the mahiṣa ritual and call out the name of the śatru;
within three full days, [the affliction] will certainly be eliminated.
If that image has been damaged, wash it clean with cow’s milk and it will immediately become as it was before.
Furthermore, as previously described, combine it with medicinal substances and so forth.
On the skin of a *caṇḍāla* insect,
write the ten-syllable Great Illuminator (*mahāvidyā*).
Afterwards, take earth from beneath the foot of a *śūdra*.
Then, take clay from the place where the mother’s *tāra* (navel) was,
mix it together, and fill it inside the skin;
bind it with human hair.
Subsequently, place the khaḷamuṇḍa and vairocana together within a single vessel and bury it deep in a cremation pit.
The vidyādhara assumes a wrathful form and,
according to the method of Mahiṣamukha,
recites the ten-syllable great mantra for one full day.
It can cause one to become a *suṇḍa*.
This rite cannot be understood.
Furthermore, take earth from seven locations where white ants have gathered.
Fashion the images of a water buffalo and a horse,
depicting them in the posture of riding one another.
Mix the blood of the water buffalo and the horse together, and as before, inscribe the Great Mantra (*mahāvidyā*).
Having placed [the remains] within the hearts of oxen and horses and buried them beneath a nimba tree,
the vidyādhara then performs the visualization.
Visualize that the *setudhara* will suffer the pain of separation from his beloved;
within three days, he will certainly be brought under control as intended.
Furthermore, as before, collect earth from seven anthills inhabited by white ants at the same locations.
Fashion it in the shape of a camel.
Following the same procedure as before, inscribe the Great Illumination (Mahāvidyā) and place it within the heart of the camel.
The Vidyādhara visualizes the syllable *baṃ*,
which becomes a wind mandala in the shape of a half-moon,
situated upon a camel.
Furthermore, one should visualize Śatru seated upon a wind-wheel;
then, visualize Yama behind Śatru,
wielding a staff to strike and drive that Śatru toward the south.
Within seven days,
that śatru will naturally depart.
Furthermore, the vidyādhara takes mustard oil.
On a day when the sun is in its great conjunction, one should smear oil upon the body of an elephant and tie it beneath a Nyagrodha tree;
subsequently, one uses oysters and clams to scrape off the oil that was applied to the elephant's body.
Later, take a banner from a temple of Maheśvara and burn it so that it does not produce flames.
Collect this smoke and mix it with the aforementioned oil.
Having smeared the feet or the garments of the *ḍākinīs*,
they depart for a short while.
Furthermore, the mantra-practitioner takes a crow’s wing to serve as a brush.
Using crow's blood as ink,
draw a wind-wheel (*vāyu-cakra*) upon birch bark;
in the center of the wind-wheel, write the name of Śatru.
Tie it to the neck of a crow.
Following the Mahiṣamukha rite, the vidyādhara performs the visualization and releases the crow toward the south.
That śabara flies away like a crow in an instant and goes far off.
Furthermore, the vidyādhara uses human feces and urine mixed together.
One should fashion an image of Śetavāsas and smear its body with powdered bone.
At midnight, the vidyādhara—
Naked, he enters a śītavana cemetery and proceeds to cut the preceding image into pieces according to the method of Mahiṣamukha.
One should perform homa within a pit for cremating corpses or at the site of a funeral pyre;
thus, that śatru will be spontaneously extinguished.
Furthermore, the vidyādhara shall use the aforementioned medicinal substances as ink.
Write the great mantra of the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka upon a shroud from a corpse. Furthermore,
use mahāpranīpa mixed with vairocana.
Fashion an image of Cakrasaṃvara;
place the previously written Great Mantra (mahāvidyā) within the heart of the image.
Then, the vidyādhara, according to the method of Mahiṣamukha, [should proceed].
Having smeared one's body with *vairocana*,
one goes to a *śītavana* (charnel ground) and cuts that image with a sharp blade before a pit for cremating corpses.
Sitting facing south, one performs the homa, and that [obstacle] will naturally be eliminated.
Furthermore, the vidyādhara takes the skin of a crow or the skin of a fox,
and upon this skin uses an iron stylus.
One should write the ten-syllable Great Illuminator mantra and write that person's name.
Then, in a secluded place, the vidyādhara should recite the ten-syllable mantra while invoking the name of Śatru.
They will naturally disperse.
Furthermore, the Vidyādhara should prepare the aforementioned medicinal substances and draw the maṇḍala of King Yama upon a shroud from a corpse.
Furthermore, one should fashion a female image from charred human bone, making its face hideous;
within the heart of the image, one places the aforementioned great mantra.
The vidyādhara then tramples upon the image with his foot.
Relying on the Mahiṣamukha rite, one should call the woman by name and recite the ten-syllable vidyā-mantra to swiftly effect her binding.
Part Three: The Section on Visualization. Furthermore, when a vidyādhara wishes to perform visualization:
First, recite the Great Mantra for Purifying the Three Karmas.
Having purified the three karmas,
one should then, with a mind free from self-clinging, [proceed].
One contemplates all phenomena as being without self.
Having contemplated all phenomena and attained the realization of non-self,
one contemplates the noble ones in accordance with the principle of suchness.
Then, from within one's own mind, one visualizes the syllable *baṃ*.
Once the syllable *baṃ* has appeared, it transforms into a wind-wheel (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).
One further visualizes that the wind-wheel is smoke-colored.
Upon that wheel, the first letter appears.
Visualize that the first letter transforms into an Indra-maṇḍala.
Upon that maṇḍala, visualize the appearance of the letter Ṭi.
Furthermore, one should visualize that the syllable *Ti* transforms into the form of the youth Mañjuśrī. Then, within the heart of the youth Mañjuśrī,
one should visualize the appearance of the syllable *A*, which transforms into a sun disc.
From within the solar disc, a great radiance issues forth,
pervading and illuminating infinite buddha-fields throughout the ten directions,
reaching the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and even the Vidyādhararājas.
Having universally illuminated those buddha-fields,
he returns once more into the interior of the solar disc.
One should thus visualize the Youthful Mañjuśrī.
It is no different and no distinct from all Tathāgatas;
within the solar disc it emits great radiance,
illuminating hundreds of thousands of yojanas.
Furthermore, one should visualize a black syllable HŪṂ appearing upon a solar disc,
surrounded on all sides by light of five colors. Then,
one should further visualize that within the light, the syllable HŪṂ transforms into a great vajra.
The black [syllable] emits a great light.
One should further visualize that vajra-wands transform and give birth to all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and vidyārājas,
as fine as sesame seeds, filling the entirety of space.
Adorned with all the primary and secondary marks and surrounded by a halo of light,
one further visualizes these Buddhas, the Tathāgatas,
each delivering sentient beings and attaining perfect enlightenment.
Having completed the deliverance of sentient beings,
he returns once more into the interior of the vajra. Furthermore,
one should visualize that from the vajra, there emanates a great Vajrapāla.
It has nine faces; the first,
the front face, has the appearance of Mahiṣamukha and is of a great black color.
On the right side, atop the śṛṅga, there are three faces:
the central face is blue, the right face is red, and the left face is yellow;
all are wrathful in appearance.
On the left side, Śṛiga also has three faces:
the central face is white, the right face is smoke-colored, and the left face is black;
all are wrathful in expression.
Between the two śṛṅgāras, he has an eighth face,
which is a great crimson color with a wrathful expression;
above that, he has a ninth face.
He assumes the form of a wrathful youth;
he is yellow in color with five topknots on his head,
and is adorned with the ornaments of a youth.
Thus, all nine faces have three eyes each;
they manifest expressions of great ferocity or loud laughter,
with tongues protruding outward and brows knitted in frowns.
Naked, with a large belly and hair standing erect,
wearing an elephant hide as a garment and adorned with skulls,
he possesses thirty-four arms.
The first right hand holds a sword;
the second hand holds a pinipāla;
the third hand holds a pestle.
The fourth hand holds a *khariga*;
the fifth hand holds a *kaṇaya*;
the sixth hand holds an axe.
The seventh hand holds a stake;
the eighth hand holds a human head;
the ninth hand holds a hook.
The tenth hand holds a jewel-staff (*ratnadaṇḍa*); the eleventh hand holds a *khaṭvāṅga*;
the twelfth hand holds a wheel (*cakra*);
and the thirteenth hand holds a vajra.
The fourteenth hand holds a vajra-mallet;
the fifteenth hand holds a sword;
the sixteenth hand holds a nāmaruka.
The first left hand holds a skull;
the second hand holds a human head;
the third hand holds a khatvāṅga.
The fourth hand holds a human foot;
the fifth hand holds a lasso;
the sixth hand holds a bow.
The seventh hand holds an *ātala*;
the eighth hand holds a bell;
the ninth hand holds a human hand.
The tenth hand holds a shroud;
the eleventh hand holds a human pin;
the twelfth hand holds a brazier.
The thirteenth hand holds a *caṣaka* cup;
the fourteenth hand performs the *kīlana-mudrā*;
the fifteenth hand holds a banner.
The sixteenth hand holds a sail;
the two hands on the left and right hold elephant hide.
It has sixteen feet.
The right first foot treads upon a human;
the second foot treads upon a water buffalo;
the third foot treads upon a yellow ox.
The fourth foot treads upon a donkey;
the fifth foot treads upon a camel;
the sixth foot treads upon a dog.
The seventh foot treads upon a sheep;
the eighth foot treads upon a wild fox;
the first left foot treads upon a vulture.
The second foot treads upon a fox;
the third foot treads upon a crow;
the fourth foot treads upon a lion.
With the fifth foot he treads upon Siṇa;
with the sixth foot he treads upon Nītra;
with the seventh foot he treads upon Mahākuna.
The eighth has his feet treading upon cranes;
his body possesses radiant flames like the fire at the end of an eon,
blazing and intense with great majestic power.
Uttering the syllable "Phaṭ" with a voice like a thunderclap,
gods and humans who hear or see it are all struck with great terror; this is the Vajrapāla.
Not only do they consume the blood, flesh, marrow, and brains of humans,
but even the various devas of the triple world fear being devoured by them.
When a vidyādhara performs visualization, [they appear].
In a secluded place,
having warded off external objects, one should focus the mind with right mindfulness and visualize the noble ones through the contemplation of the principle of suchness.
Having brought [the vision] before oneself,
one perceives that the bodies of the noble ones are one's own body;
having attained this, one abides in fearlessness.
Again, one visualizes a solar disc appearing within the heart;
upon that solar disc, one contemplates the syllable of Great Radiance (*mahāvidyā*).
Once this syllable has appeared, it emits light that shines forth in the four directions.
The Vidyādhara should perform visualization in this manner;
once accomplishment is attained, one may then engage in recitation.
During the time of recitation, one should constantly consume the five kinds of nectar-medicines.
And having recited the root mantra of Mahāpratiṣā three hundred thousand times,
once that number is complete—
Thereafter, one should perform the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
If one follows the ritual manual (*vidhi*) without error,
one will certainly achieve accomplishment in all dharmas.
Section Four: The Ritual for Painting Images. Regarding the ritual for painting images: when a vidyādhara wishes to paint an image of the Lord Mahāvajrapāla, [he should proceed as follows].
One should first seek out a skillful painter;
that painter must be pure and free from the faults of indolence or disrespect.
Possessing a mind of compassion, patience, and faith,
once such a person of virtue has been found,
the vidyādhara shall provide the artist with whatever wages they request.
One should give whatever is requested without bargaining for the price.
Once a painter has been obtained, the mantra-practitioner may then seek the robes of a person who is courageous and upright.
If a woman comes seeking clothing for concealment or touching,
or requests clothing for childbirth, one should provide such garments;
if these are unavailable, one should instead use shrouds from a corpse.
Having obtained the cloth,
one should immediately go to a secluded place where there are no people and have the painter select an auspicious day to begin drawing the image on the scroll.
Except for the vidyādhara and the painter,
no other persons whatsoever shall see it; if one allows others to see it,
the ritual practice will not be accomplished.
As for the form of Mahāvajraprāvara:
he has one body with nine faces, is naked and black in color,
possesses thirty-four arms and sixteen legs.
The first face is black with the *mahīśamukha* (buffalo-head) mark.
Above the right shoulder (*śṛṅga*) are three faces:
the central one is blue, the right is red, and the left is yellow; all are wrathful in appearance.
On the left side, the śṛṅga also has three faces:
the central one is white, the right is smoke-colored, and the left is black.
Between the two śṛṅgas, the eighth face is painted red.
Above the eighth face, draw the ninth face,
depicting the form of Mañjuśrī-kumāra, yellow in color;
thus, all nine faces are wrathful in appearance.
He possesses thirty-four hands.
The first right hand holds a sword; the second hand holds a *pinipāla*;
the third hand holds a pestle; and the fourth hand holds a *kharika*.
The fifth hand holds a *kaṇaya*, the sixth hand holds a great axe,
the seventh hand holds a spear, the eighth hand holds an arrow,
the ninth hand holds a hook, and the tenth hand holds a jeweled staff.
The eleventh hand holds a khakkhara staff; the twelfth hand holds a wheel;
the thirteenth hand holds a vajra; and the fourteenth hand holds a *ghaṇṭā* (bell).
The fifteenth hand holds a sharp sword; the sixteenth hand holds a *nāmaruka* fruit.
The first left hand holds a skull-cup;
the second hand holds a human head.
The third hand holds a *kīlaka*; the fourth hand holds a human foot;
the fifth hand holds a noose (*pāśa*); the sixth hand holds a bow;
the seventh hand holds an *ṛṣṭi*; and the eighth hand holds a bell (*ghaṇṭā*).
The ninth hand holds a human hand; the tenth hand holds a shroud from a corpse.
The eleventh hand holds a *śalākā* (lot); the twelfth hand forms the *samaya-mudrā*.
The thirteenth hand holds a *caṣaka* (cup); the fourteenth hand performs the *samaya-mudrā*.
The fifteenth hand holds a banner, and the sixteenth hand holds a sail.
The two hands on either side hold elephant hide.
The first right foot treads upon a human, and the second right foot treads upon a water buffalo.
The third foot treads upon a yellow ox; the fourth foot treads upon a donkey;
the fifth foot treads upon a camel; the sixth foot treads upon a dog;
the seventh foot treads upon a sheep; and the eighth foot treads upon a wild fox.
The first left foot treads upon a vulture; the second foot treads upon a fox;
the third foot treads upon a crow; the fourth foot treads upon a lion;
the fifth foot treads upon a *siṃha* bird; and the sixth foot treads upon a *nīdara*.
The seventh foot treads upon a mahāśakuna bird; the eighth foot treads upon a śarabha.
In front of the image, one should draw a śmaśāna (charnel ground), within which are various rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, and so forth.
Furthermore, one should paint a nyagrodha tree,
upon which human corpses are suspended and pinned;
below the tree in the forest, one should also paint the corpses of many people.
There are various kinds of flying birds, foxes, dogs, and others with the appearance of devouring many corpses.
In front of the principal deity, one should draw the vidyādhara,
naked and with disheveled hair, wearing a crown of skulls.
Anointing one's body with the five kinds of nectar-medicines,
and holding a *nāmaruka* fruit and a skull-topped *khaṭvāṅga* staff in hand,
one gazes upon the *pīṭhaja* (born of the sacred seats) deity.
With a face again breaking into a great laugh, he proceeds into the Śītavana charnel ground.
Once the painting of the image has been completed in this manner,
place this scroll in a deep, secret, and tranquil location.
One should constantly burn human flesh as incense for offering.
The Vidyādhara uses human bone for a rosary.
Before this image, one should focus the mind with devotion three times each day.
Recite the great mantra three hundred thousand times (*tri-lakṣa*).
Thereafter, perform the ritual according to one’s wish; success will be certain.
This painted scroll image must not be entrusted to others.
Furthermore, one must not casually display it before others so that they may gaze upon it.
The Vidyādhara takes wine and meat as food;
moreover, three times each day, he uses *vairocana* mixed with human blood as incense.
Burn [the substances] before the painting as an offering.
One who practices with such sincerity and without retreat will certainly attain the supreme accomplishment.

5. The Section on the Homa Ritual, Part Five. Furthermore, when a vidyādhara wishes to perform the homa ritual to seek accomplishment, he must first, in advance, recite the root mantra of his chosen deity until the preliminary practice is fully perfected.
Thereafter, having prepared the required fuel and all other materials according to the ritual procedure and having completed these preparations,
the vidyādhara shall, during the night, take the various homa substances.
Go alone to the śmaśāna forest and seek accomplishment according to the ritual method.
Once you have attained siddhi, thereafter perform all rites as you wish.
Furthermore, the vidyādhara,
before Vajrapaira, recites the great mantra while using human flesh mixed with wine.
Performing the homa one hundred and eight times every day for a full six months,
the vidyādhara shall attain mahāsiddhi.
Furthermore, if a vidyādhara wishes to seek great power and the affection and respect of kings and the common people,
he should practice according to the method of Mahiṣamukha.
Seated upright, he should visualize himself as Peḷava.
Holding a hook and a lasso in his hands,
one further visualizes Mañjuśrī emanating from within this body and proceeding to the place where the person to be subdued resides.
Draw that person in and cause them to enter within one's own body.
Furthermore, visualize the ten-syllable Great Mantra in red,
appearing within that person's heart like the sign of great wisdom.
When the vidyādhara performs this rite,
even those of extreme power may be rendered submissive through love; indeed,
throughout his entire life, everything shall be accomplished according to his will.
Furthermore, when a vidyādhara wishes to perform the rite of pacification (śāntika),
he should construct a fire pit before an image of Peḷava and sit facing east within the pit.
Burn *palāśa* wood fuel,
mixed with clarified butter, honey, and *nṛvaja* grass;
recite the Great Mantra while performing *homā* one hundred and eight times.
Even the cities and kingdoms will have their calamities pacified.
Furthermore, when a vidyādhara performs a rite of augmentation (puṣṭika),
he should sit facing east and visualize the deity.
Having attained presence,
one should immediately burn *udumbara* wood in the hearth,
using sesame seeds, white non-glutinous rice, and clarified butter mixed together.
If one performs the homa three times a day for a thousand repetitions,
one will swiftly attain increase.
Furthermore, if a vidyādhara wishes to perform subjugation:
Using peacock, jackal, snake, crow, horse, buffalo, and other *piśācas*,
as well as hair, grain chaff, and other such substances as medicine,
one should recite the name [of the deceased] within the fire used for cremation.
One who recites the great mantra and performs homa will swiftly bring [the target] under control.
Alternatively, one may take firewood remaining from a cremation or obtain fire from the house of a candāla.
If one recites the Great Mantra while performing homa within one's own residence while calling out the name of the person,
that person will also be subdued within seven days.
One who performs this rite may even subdue Vajrasattva himself.
Furthermore, for a vidyādhara who intends to act against a śatru,
one should use human bone, vīraja, gairika, bālana, and śveta-naraka.
Together with thorns, hair, nails, and so forth,
mix them with oil; then,
before the pit for cremating the corpse, [perform the ritual].
Sit facing south,
recite the Great Mantra (Mahāvidyā) one hundred and eight times while calling out the name [of the person].
Within three days, that Śatru will be eliminated.
Alternatively, in a deep, secret, and tranquil place,
construct a triangular hearth;
all other materials and procedures are the same as previously described.
Performing one hundred and eight homas will likewise eliminate it.
Furthermore, when a vidyādhara wishes to dispatch a śatru,
he should use the flesh of a crow and the dung of a camel.
Mixing [the substances] with liquor,
the vidyādhara, naked and with hair disheveled,
enters the śmaśāna forest and sits facing south before a pit for cremating corpses.
First, visualize the wind mandala, and then visualize a śatru atop the wind mandala.
Once this has been clearly visualized before you,
take the aforementioned items and place them within the fire used for cremating corpses.
If one performs one thousand *homa* offerings, [the obstacle] will quickly depart on its own.
Furthermore, regarding the rite for the dismissal of the *śatru*:
one should use crow meat mixed with rice bran.
Burn *mandāra* wood together with [the substance] to perform *homa* for seven days, and it will depart of its own accord.
Furthermore, use the flesh of a crow to perform *homa* one thousand times as before for three days, and it will depart of its own accord.
Furthermore, the Vidyādhara takes beef and blood,
recites the Great Mantra while calling out the name [of the target],
and performs one thousand oblations (homa).
One should cause the person referred to by name to quickly come, submit, and serve.
Alternatively, using dog meat and *vajrodaka* (vajra-water),
one should perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings during the night.
They will also swiftly come to submit and offer precious jewels.
Alternatively, one may use horse meat mixed with vairocana at night in a secluded place.
Perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings;
by the seventh day, a king and all people will be completely subdued.
Alternatively, use elephant meat mixed with *śukara* (pig) meat.
If one performs homa during the night for seven days,
all people will be brought under control.
Furthermore, the vidyādhara may perform homa using meat and fish mixed with wine.
All Sitātalis shall come and be subdued.
Furthermore, the vidyādhara should visualize the bodies of a man and a woman as red in color;
reciting their names and chanting the great mantra, he should sit facing west.
Burn *khadira* wood fuel,
using sesame seeds and white non-glutinous rice,
mixed with *vajra-water*, performing the homa for seven days.
They come of their own accord to be subdued, approached, and served.
Furthermore, perform the rite of summoning by fashioning an image of the person using mustard seeds.
If one performs homa for seven days in a fire of khadira wood,
the one summoned will certainly arrive.

Alternatively, one may mix five kinds of nectar-medicines with clarified butter and perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings in a fire of *khadira* wood; thus, the summoned deity will swiftly arrive.

6. The Section on the Accomplishment through Visualization. Sixth. Furthermore, when a Vidyādhara wishes to perform this rite, he must first practice this visualization until it is thoroughly mastered.
Thereafter, one performs the ritual procedure.
Furthermore, when a vidyādhara wishes to eliminate a śatru,
he should rely on the method of Mahiṣamukha.
Once the visualization of the syllable RA has become clearly manifest before one,
it immediately transforms into a wheel of fire with blazing flames.
Upon this wheel of fire, visualize Śatru.
Appearing with a naked body, disheveled hair,
and a frail appearance, the Vidyādhara further emanates a wrathful vidyārāja from within his own body.
Holding a sharp sword in his hand, he cuts off the body, flesh, and blood of the śatru and devours them;
one should perform the visualization that the śatru will certainly be thus eliminated.
If one recites the great mantra for seven days,
not only can ordinary beings, but even Vajrasattva himself, be purified and cleansed.
Furthermore, the vidyādhara first visualizes his own body.
Having performed the *mahīṣamukha* [visualization] as before,
one should likewise visualize a great wheel of fire;
upon that wheel of fire, one visualizes Śatru.
Visualize the appearance of being terrified,
trembling, and agitated. Furthermore, imagine that malevolent rākṣasas are devouring those śatrus,
followed by the appearance of crows, vultures, foxes, dogs, and the like, all vying with one another to come and devour them.
That *piśāca* will constantly destroy itself.
Furthermore, the mantra-practitioner (*vidyādhara*) performs the rite of dismissal:
first, he visualizes the syllable *baṃ*.
Once it has appeared before one, it immediately transforms into a half-moon-shaped wind-wheel.
One should visualize Śvetaketu upon this wind-wheel,
naked with disheveled hair and appearing emaciated.
The Vidyādhara visualizes himself as Mahiṣamukha,
likewise standing upon a wind-wheel;
he then visualizes the wind-wheel transforming into a camel.
Visualize the appearance of Śatru riding a camel and departing to the south.
Furthermore, visualize King Yama with disheveled hair,
holding a precious staff in his hand.
Thereafter, strike it.
If one performs this visualization for seven days,
not only ordinary beings but even sages and worthies can be dispatched.
Furthermore, the vidyādhara, relying on the mahiṣamukha rite,
sits upright in meditation and visualizes Setu riding either upon a vulture or a crow.
Furthermore, one should visualize King Yama,
holding a staff in his right hand and grasping [the deceased's] hair with his left,
casting them toward the south.
Maintaining this visualization for seven days,
there is nothing that will not be dispatched.
Furthermore, when a Vidyādhara wishes to remove the great poison of snakebites, [he should perform this].
First, visualize one's own mind as an eight-petaled white lotus flower;
imagine that upon it is the third seed-syllable,
which then transforms into one's own body.
It is white.
Again, visualize a single syllable appearing upon the crown of the head;
from within that single syllable, nectar flows forth.
One should perform the consecration for the person bitten by a venomous creature.
Furthermore, one should visualize an eight-petaled lotus,
within the eight petals of which appear the eight great nāga kings.
From the eyes of the nāgas, ambrosia further emerges;
it is poured upon the bodies of those bitten by snakes.
When this rite is performed, it reaches the great poisons that fill the three realms.
It can also eliminate [the effects of] retrogression. If a vidyādhara performs this rite,
even if he consumes a great poison himself, it will cause him no harm.
At that time, the Great Vajrapāṇi,
having spoken these various ritual procedures,
again addressed the assembly, saying:
Do not violate what I have previously admonished you;
if you do violate it, you shall incur calamity and retribution in this life,
and subsequently suffer immeasurable retribution in hell.
Having spoken these words, Peḷava prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew.
[Thus ends] the *Sūtra on the Ritual for the Accomplishment of the Visualization of the Great Vajra Peḷava Wheel of the Great Teaching of Mañjuśrī Yoga*.
